source_refs.note: Chapter opening and topic 10.1, printed pages 215-221: the respiratory surface, the upper and lower tracts, the alveoli, the mechanism of breathing and its control.

blocks.text: Organisms get energy out of food molecules by catabolic processes in their cells, collectively called cellular respiration (glycolysis, the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain), which use oxygen and produce carbon dioxide. External respiration is the uptake of oxygen from the environment and the disposal of carbon dioxide into it at the body-system level; it involves breathing and the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide in the capillaries. The organs that carry out these processes constitute the respiratory system. Its main organs are the lungs, which provide a suitable respiratory surface for gas exchange.

blocks.title: Recalling
blocks.text: Our cells obtain oxygen from the blood, and the blood obtains it from the air in our lungs. Oxygen diffuses across the wet membranes of the lungs, which are filled with air in the process of breathing.
Properties of the respiratory surface

The respiratory surface is the area where actual gas exchange occurs between the environment and the blood, by diffusion. In humans and other air-breathing vertebrates, oxygen from the air diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood to the air. Seven properties enable respiratory surfaces to exchange gases effectively.

items: It is moist and permeable, so that gases may pass through it.
It is thin, so that gases travel the minimum distance.
It has a blood supply, so that gases can diffuse into and out of the blood.
It has structural support, so that it remains open and does not collapse.
It is located internally, so that its moist surface does not lose water to the atmosphere.
Air ventilates over it, moving towards and away from it.
Air reaches it after passing a branched tubular way, so that it is saturated with water vapour before arriving.

blocks.text: Components of the human respiratory system

The organs of the respiratory system form a continuous system of passages, the respiratory tract, through which air flows into and out of the body. The tract has two major divisions, the upper respiratory tract and the lower respiratory tract.
Upper respiratory tract
The upper tract consists of the nasal cavity, pharynx and larynx. These organs move air into and out of the body and also clean, humidify and warm the incoming air; no gas exchange occurs in them.

items: Nasal cavity: the external openings of the nose, the nostrils, lead to a large air-filled space behind the nose, partitioned by the nasal septum (a part of the nasal bone). As inhaled air flows through it, blood vessels very close to its surface warm and humidify it, and hairs in the nose and mucus from the mucous membranes trap larger foreign particles before they go deeper. The nasal cavity also contains the chemoreceptors needed for the sense of smell, which contribute to the sense of taste.

Pharynx: a tube-like structure connecting the nasal and oral cavities to the larynx and oesophagus. Both air and food pass through it, so it belongs to both the respiratory and digestive systems: air passes from the nasal cavity through the pharynx to the larynx (and back), and food from the mouth through the pharynx to the oesophagus.

Larynx: connects the pharynx and trachea and is composed of muscles and cartilages. It is also called the voice box because it contains two bands of smooth muscle, the vocal cords, which vibrate when air flows over them and so produce sound. Muscles in the larynx move the vocal cords apart to allow breathing, and other muscles move them together to produce vocal sounds and control their pitch and volume.

The epiglottis is a cartilaginous flap that extends in front of and above the opening of the larynx, the glottis. When air enters the larynx the epiglottis stands upwards to give way to it. When we swallow, the backward motion of the tongue raises the larynx, which forces the epiglottis downwards to close the glottis and prevents swallowed material from entering the larynx.

blocks.title: The cough reflex
blocks.text: If swallowed material does start to enter the larynx, it irritates the larynx and stimulates a strong cough reflex, which generally expels the material out of the larynx into the throat.
Lower respiratory tract

The trachea and the other passages of the lower tract conduct air between the upper tract and the lungs. They branch repeatedly into a tree-like shape; there are an astonishing 2,414 kilometres of airways conducting air through the human respiratory tract. It is only in the lungs, however, that gas exchange between air and blood occurs.

blocks.alt: The trachea runs down between the two lungs and divides into two bronchi, which branch again and again inside the right and left lungs like the branches of an upside-down tree.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.4: Tree-like branching of the lower respiratory tract (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.4).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Trachea, Right lung, Left lung.

items: Trachea: the windpipe connects the larynx to the lungs and is the widest passageway in the tract, about 1 inch wide and 4 to 6 inches long. Its walls are made of smooth muscle and C-shaped rings of cartilage, which give strength and support to keep the passage open. It is lined with mucus and cilia; the cilia propel foreign particles trapped in the mucus towards the pharynx. At the bottom the trachea branches into two bronchi.

Bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli: the two primary bronchi (singular bronchus) enter the lungs and branch into smaller secondary bronchi, two in the left lung and three in the right. In the secondary bronchi the C-shaped cartilages are replaced by cartilage plates. They branch into still smaller tertiary bronchi, which branch further into very small bronchioles, which have no cartilage plates. The bronchioles divide many times into terminal bronchioles, which end in alveolar ducts that terminate in clusters of tiny air sacs, the alveoli (singular alveolus).

Lungs: the largest organs of the tract. Each lung is covered by two membranes: the visceral pleura lines the lung and the parietal pleura lines the inner wall of the thoracic cavity. The small space between them, the pleural cavity, is filled with fluid that lets the lungs expand and contract freely during breathing. Each lung is divided into lobes: the right lung is larger with three lobes, the left smaller with two, leaving room for the heart just left of the centre of the chest.

blocks.alt: The trachea divides into primary bronchi, which branch into secondary and tertiary bronchi inside the lungs. The right lung (left of the picture) has superior, middle and inferior lobes; the smaller left lung has superior and inferior lobes and a cardiac notch in its lower inner edge.

blocks.text: Alveoli

Each alveolar duct opens into a cluster of 20 to 30 alveoli. These clusters make up the bulk of the lung and are surrounded by blood capillaries. An alveolus is made of moist epithelial tissue only 0.1 micrometre thick, so the alveoli provide the respiratory surface where gas exchange takes place between air and blood. The alveoli are the functional units of the lungs; the two lungs may contain as many as 700 million, giving a huge total surface area. When we breathe in, the alveoli fill with air and the lungs expand; oxygen in the alveolar air is absorbed by diffusion into the network of tiny capillaries around them, and the blood in those capillaries releases carbon dioxide, also by diffusion, into the alveolar air. When we breathe out, the air leaves the alveoli for the atmosphere, carrying the carbon dioxide with it.

blocks.title: Surfactant and the blood supply of the lungs
blocks.text: Some epithelial cells of the alveoli secrete a liquid called surfactant, which lines the inside of the alveoli and prevents them from collapsing and sticking together when air moves out; in healthy lungs it is constantly secreted and reabsorbed. The pulmonary arteries carry deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where it absorbs oxygen, and the pulmonary veins carry the oxygenated blood back to the heart to be pumped through the body. The lungs also receive oxygenated blood from the heart for the cellular respiration of their own cells.

blocks.text: Mechanism of breathing or ventilation

The movement of air into and out of the body is breathing or ventilation. Our lungs do not draw in air or push it out; this is done by creating negative and positive pressures in the lungs, through two sets of muscles: the diaphragm, a dome-like large skeletal muscle that separates the thoracic cavity from the abdomen, and the intercostal muscles between each pair of ribs.

items: Inspiration (inhalation), taking in air: the diaphragm contracts, which lowers it and gives it a more flattened shape, and at the same time the intercostal muscles contract, raising the ribs and expanding the rib cage. These contractions increase the space in the thorax, so the lungs expand because of the adherence of the visceral and parietal pleural membranes. The expansion lowers the air pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric pressure, and air enters.

Expiration (exhalation), moving air out: the expansion of the thorax and lungs during inspiration places them under elastic tension, which is relieved when the intercostal muscles and diaphragm relax. The diaphragm resumes its dome shape and, as the intercostal muscles relax, the ribs lower and the rib cage moves inward. These movements decrease the space in the thorax and let the lungs recoil, so the pressure inside the lungs rises above atmospheric pressure and air moves out.

blocks.alt: Two front views of the chest. Inspiration (inhalation): air moves in through the trachea; red arrows show the rib cage moving outward and the flattened diaphragm moving down, and the lungs are larger. Expiration (exhalation): air moves out; arrows show the rib cage moving inward and the domed diaphragm moving up, and the lungs are smaller.
blocks.caption: Figure 10.7: Mechanism of breathing (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 10.7).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Air moves in; Intercostal muscles contract and rib cage expands; Lung; Diaphragm; Diaphragm contracts (moves down); Inspiration (Inhalation); Air moves out; Intercostal muscles relax and rib cage becomes smaller; Diaphragm relaxes (moves up); Expiration (Exhalation).

blocks.title: High altitudes and birds
blocks.text: Atmospheric pressure is lower at high altitudes, so a greater increase in the thorax is needed to make the lung pressure lower than atmospheric, which is why breathing is harder there; the body adapts to improve oxygen uptake, which is why athletes often train at high altitude before competitions. Birds have lungs and air sacs, and air flows in one direction, from outside to the posterior air sacs, then to the lungs, the anterior air sacs and out, opposite to the blood flow, so gas exchange is much more efficient and birds obtain enough oxygen even at high altitudes.

blocks.alt: A bird in side view, drawn twice. In each, the trachea runs into the chest to the lungs; anterior air sacs lie in front of the lungs and posterior air sacs behind them. At inhalation the air sacs are full (larger); at exhalation they are smaller.
blocks.caption: Air sacs and lungs of a bird (original drawing after the drawing in the textbook's High altitudes and birds box).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Anterior air sacs, Posterior air sacs, Lungs, Inhalation, Exhalation.

blocks.text: Control of breathing

Each breath is initiated by neurons in a respiratory centre in the medulla oblongata, a part of the brain stem. These neurons send impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, stimulating them to contract and causing inspiration. When the neurons stop producing impulses, the diaphragm and intercostal muscles relax and expiration occurs.
